narrative:
The model estimates a 46% chance that you will leave your current job. Because this probability is high enough to flag you as a likely departure, the organization has decided to deny your promotion.

The decision was driven primarily by three key aspects of your profile. First, the fact that you have received other job opportunities while at the company was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward leaving. Most employees the model expects to stay have not been approached by outside employers, so this makes you stand out as more mobile. Second, your six to ten years of experience in your current role also pulled the prediction toward departure. While this tenure is fairly common among those predicted to stay, the model sees it as a point where many professionals begin to consider new horizons. Third, your overall career experience of six to ten years worked in the opposite direction, modestly encouraging the model to expect you to stay; however, this positive influence was not strong enough to outweigh the first two factors.

Taken together, the combination of external opportunities and solid time already spent in the role outweighed your broader experience and created enough concern about retention that the organization chose not to promote you at this time.

You and your manager should discuss what would make staying more attractive. Addressing recognition, rewards, or workload balance could reduce the pull of outside offers and help you build a longer future here.
